title: Operation Southbound Takedown: 13 charged in stolen-car pipeline to Mexico cartels
excerpt: Federal prosecutors say 13 people are charged in Operation Southbound Takedown, accused of moving stolen cars through El Paso into Mexico, where investigators say cartels used them.
content:
Federal prosecutors in El Paso have charged 13 people accused of feeding a cross-border pipeline of stolen vehicles to criminal organizations in Mexico, in a case that lands close to home for Laredo drivers who were warned this week about high-tech push-to-start thefts.

The case, announced October 26 by U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas, is called Operation Southbound Takedown. Investigators say 29 vehicles valued at about $1.137 million have been recovered. The vehicles were allegedly stolen from private owners and rental fleets in cities across the United States, from Florida to California, and driven through El Paso into Mexico.

All 13 defendants are charged with interstate transportation of stolen property, which carries up to 10 years in federal prison if convicted. Eleven are U.S. citizens and two are Mexican nationals, prosecutors said; two defendants were in state custody, while the other 11 were federally indicted and arrested between July 22 and October 19.

Homeland Security Investigations, the FBI and other agencies worked the case through the Homeland Security Task Force. Investigators say the probe began in spring 2026 after agents noticed a pattern of stolen private and rental vehicles being delivered to people allegedly connected to criminal organizations in Mexico.

Federal officials say the recovered vehicles included large SUVs later converted for cartel use, and that authorities linked the pipeline to groups operating around Juárez. The charging documents made public so far focus on stolen-property transport, not on drug counts, and prosecutors have not publicly detailed each defendant's alleged role.

Why it matters in Webb County: Laredo sits on the same border corridor, and local police warned October 29-30 about push-to-start theft rings that can take a vehicle in about a minute using handheld programming tools. A federal case that recovers 29 vehicles is a reminder that a stolen car here is rarely just a local theft — it can be inventory for an organization across the border.

The charges are allegations, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. Webb Watch 956 will follow the El Paso proceedings and any Laredo-linked theft cases that emerge from them.
